B3C1: Foreword introducing Book Three: having shown God as first being and beginning of all things, Aquinas turns to God as the end of all things, the theme this book will pursue.
B3C2: Every agent, in acting, intends an end; the movement of any cause toward an effect is directed toward something, whether the agent knows it or not, as arrow to target.
B3C3: Since every agent acts for an end, and ends have the nature of good, it follows that every agent, in acting, acts for a good, never for evil as such.
B3C4: Because every agent acts for a good, evil that results from action is always beside the agent's intention; nothing intends evil as such, so evil is incidental to things.
B3C5: States and answers objections claiming evil sometimes seems intended directly, such as when agents cause corruption or a stronger cause destroys a weaker one's form.
B3C6: Continues resolving objections that evil is not beside intention, showing that even destructive natural processes and voluntary evildoing pursue an apparent good, not evil itself.
B3C7: Evil is not a positive essence or nature but a privation of due good in a subject; it names an absence, not a thing existing in its own right.
B3C8: Presents arguments seeming to show evil is a real nature or thing, such as evil's contrariety to good and its capacity to corrupt, which will be answered afterward.
B3C9: Continues objections that evil might be a genuine nature, addressing appearances that evil acts as a cause and has degrees, preparing the ground for rebuttal.
B3C10: Since evil is privation in a good subject, and privation presupposes a subject, the cause of evil is always found to be some good acting defectively.
B3C11: Evil always exists in a good subject, since privation requires an underlying substance capable of the good it lacks; there is no evil apart from some good.
B3C12: However much evil increases, it cannot wholly destroy good, since evil's subject is itself good and would vanish along with its own foothold if good were annihilated.
B3C13: Although evil has no cause per se, since nothing seeks evil as such, every evil must nonetheless have some accidental cause arising from a defective good agent.
B3C14: Evil is shown to be strictly an accidental cause of further effects, since whatever accompanies a per se good cause can itself accidentally cause corresponding evil results.
B3C15: There can be no single sovereign evil serving as first principle of all evils, since evil always presupposes and depends upon some good as its subject and cause.
B3C16: Since every agent acts for some good, as already shown, it follows universally that good is the end toward which everything, in acting, ultimately tends.
B3C17: All things are directed to one single ultimate good as their last end, and that supreme good toward which the whole order of the universe tends is God.
B3C19: Because creatures acquire likeness to God by tending toward His goodness as their last end, the ultimate end of all things is to become like unto God.
B3C20: Since the end properly has the nature of good, creatures imitate God specifically insofar as He is good, each striving after its own share of divine goodness.
B3C21: Things also tend to be like God insofar as He is a cause, since creatures are naturally inclined to produce effects and thereby communicate their own goodness to others.
B3C22: Things are directed to their proper ends chiefly through their proper operations, so the last means of reaching an end for any given thing is its characteristic activity.
B3C23: The movement of the heavens proceeds from an intellective principle, since ordered, purposeful celestial motion cannot arise from a merely natural, unknowing cause acting for an end.
B3C24: Since the heavenly bodies are moved by an intelligent substance for the sake of generation below, even things devoid of knowledge seek the good through the intention of that governing intelligence.
B3C25: Because all creatures reach God as their end through some likeness to Him, intellectual creatures attain Him specially by their proper operation, so to know God is their true end.
B3C26: Considers whether happiness consists in an act of the will, namely loving God, rather than in intellectual knowledge of Him, weighing arguments on both sides before resolving the question.
B3C27: Human happiness cannot consist in bodily pleasures, chief among them those of food and sex, since these are common to beasts and do not fulfill man's highest, rational nature.
B3C28: Happiness does not consist in honours, since man's ultimate good must be his own most perfect operation, whereas honour is something bestowed on him externally by others.
B3C29: Man's happiness does not consist in glory, the mere recognition or renown of one's good name among others, since this too is extrinsic and dependent on others' opinion.
B3C30: Wealth cannot be man's supreme good, since riches are sought only for the sake of something else and are properly valued in their spending rather than their possession.
B3C31: Worldly power cannot be man's ultimate happiness, being unstable, subject to chance, often held by evil men, and not itself constituting a person as good or evil.
B3C32: Bodily goods such as health, beauty and strength cannot be man's supreme good, since they are shared with the wicked, are unstable, and lie outside control of the will.
B3C33: Human happiness is not seated in the goods of the sensitive faculty, since such pleasures and perfections are common to man and irrational animals alike.
B3C34: Man's ultimate happiness does not consist in acts of moral virtue, since moral action is ordered further to contemplation and cannot itself be the final, ultimate end.
B3C35: Ultimate happiness does not consist in the act of prudence, since prudence directs action toward further ends and so cannot itself be man's final resting end.
B3C36: Happiness cannot consist in the practice of art, since artistic knowledge is likewise practical, ordered to producing something beyond itself, and therefore not an ultimate end.
B3C37: Having excluded external, bodily, sensitive, and practical-intellectual goods, Aquinas concludes that man's ultimate happiness consists in contemplation, specifically the contemplating of truth, above all divine truth.
B3C38: The vague, general knowledge of God possessed naturally by nearly everyone through natural reason does not suffice for ultimate happiness, since it remains confused and imperfect.
B3C39: Even the more precise, demonstrative knowledge of God attained through philosophical proof, however superior to common opinion, still falls short of constituting man's final happiness.
B3C40: The knowledge of God given through faith, though surpassing demonstration in what it reveals, still cannot constitute man's ultimate happiness since it remains obscure, not vision.
B3C41: Examines whether man in this life could attain happiness by understanding separate substances through study of speculative science, weighing the view before it is later refuted.
B3C42: Refutes Alexander of Aphrodisias's opinion that man could understand separate substances in this life through the possible intellect conceived as a corruptible disposition of human nature.
B3C43: Refutes Averroes's theory that man understands separate substances in this life by union with a single incorruptible separate possible intellect shared by all humans.
B3C44: Man's ultimate happiness cannot consist in knowledge of separate substances as proposed by Alexander or Averroes, since neither theory offers a genuine, personal human vision of such substances.
B3C45: Since separate substances cannot be known in this life by the ways previously proposed, Aquinas inquires whether they can be understood by us here at all.
B3C46: Answering an objection from Augustine, Aquinas shows the soul in this life does not understand itself, or thereby other separate substances, by itself alone apart from sense images.
B3C47: Since we cannot understand separate substances in this life owing to the intellect's dependence on phantasms, still less can we see the divine essence in this present life.
B3C48: Since ultimate happiness requires a knowledge of God beyond any attainable in this present life, it follows that man's ultimate happiness cannot be reached in this life.
B3C49: Separate substances and souls after death do not see God in His essence merely through knowing Him by way of their own created essences; a higher vision is required.
B3C50: The natural desire of separate substances for beatitude is not satisfied by the natural knowledge of God they possess through their own essences alone, but seeks more.
B3C52: No created substance, however excellent, can by its own natural power attain to seeing God in His essence; such vision requires a further, supernatural elevation by grace.
B3C54: States and resolves objections claiming God cannot be seen in His essence, such as that no added light can enable sight to exceed its natural corporeal capacity.
B3C55: The created intellect, even when granted the beatific vision, does not comprehend the divine substance fully, since its mode of knowing remains proportioned to a finite created power.
B3C56: No created intellect, in seeing God, thereby sees everything that can be seen in Him, since comprehending all His effects would require comprehending the divine essence itself.
B3C57: Every intellect, however lowly by nature, is capable of being raised by supernatural light to participate in some degree in the vision of the divine substance.
B3C58: Since the mode of the beatific vision follows the degree of participated light received, it is possible for one blessed soul to see God more perfectly than another.
B3C59: Because the vision of God is the last end that brings full rest to the intellect's natural desire to know all things, those who see God thereby see all things in Him.
B3C60: Those who see the divine substance see all things in it not successively but all at once in a single, simultaneous act of vision corresponding to that one vision.
B3C61: By seeing God, the created intellect becomes a partaker of eternal life, since that vision occurs outside time's succession and shares in the simultaneous wholeness of eternity.
B3C62: Those who attain the vision of God will possess it forever, since what is measured by eternity rather than time cannot be lost once truly possessed.
B3C64: Having shown God is the end of all things, it follows that God, by His providence, governs and rules all things, directing them toward their proper ends.
B3C65: Because God governs all things by His providence, it follows that He also continually preserves all things in existence, sustaining them from moment to moment.
B3C66: All inferior agents give existence to their effects only insofar as they act by the power of God, who alone is the primary and universal cause of being.
B3C67: In every operation performed by creatures, God is the underlying cause of their acting, since nothing operates or produces being except by sharing in God's power.
B3C68: Because God causes and sustains the being and operation of all things directly, it follows that God is present everywhere, in all things, without exception.
B3C69: Examines and rejects the opinion of those who deny creatures any proper causal activity of their own, claiming God alone directly produces all natural effects.
B3C70: Explains how one and the same natural effect can be attributed both to God as first cause and to the natural agent as true secondary cause without contradiction.
B3C71: Divine providence, though it governs all things, does not entirely exclude corruption, defects, and evil from the world, since these can arise from deficiencies in secondary causes.
B3C72: Just as providence does not banish evil from the world entirely, neither does it exclude contingency from things or impose strict necessity upon all events.
B3C73: Divine providence governing all things does not exclude free will in rational creatures, since God's governance works through and preserves the proper mode of each cause.
B3C74: Divine providence likewise does not remove chance or luck from the world, since it operates through the natural order of causes, some of which meet accidentally.
B3C75: Divine providence extends to and is concerned with singular, individual contingent things, reaching down to particulars among things subject to generation and corruption, not merely universals.
B3C76: Refuting a Platonic scheme of graded providences, Aquinas shows God's providence cares for all individuals immediately, not merely through intermediary causes or lesser gods.
B3C77: Although providence's execution is carried out through secondary causes, its ordering belongs properly to God alone, who as the wisest orders all things down to particulars.
B3C78: God rules other creatures by means of intellectual creatures, since a proportionate descending order requires the highest beings, the intellectual ones, to govern those beneath them.
B3C79: Since some intellectual creatures rank higher than others, the lower intellectual substances, such as lesser angels, are governed and ruled by the higher ones among them.
B3C80: Discusses the hierarchical order existing among angels themselves, whereby higher angelic substances, possessing more universal power, are unattached to bodies and govern the lower.
B3C82: Just as higher intellectual substances govern lower ones, inferior corporeal bodies are ruled by God through the mediation of the higher heavenly bodies above them.
B3C83: Summarizes the preceding chapters: God governs the ordering of all things by Himself alone, but executes that order through higher creatures acting upon lower ones.
B3C84: The heavenly bodies cannot directly impress themselves upon our intellect, since the order of providence requires higher things, and the intellect surpasses all corporeal natures.
B3C85: The heavenly bodies are not the cause of our acts of willing and choosing, since the will, like the intellect, transcends direct corporeal causal influence.
B3C86: Corporeal effects in the lower world do not follow of strict necessity from the action of the heavenly bodies, since matter's disposition can impede their influence.
B3C87: Rejects Avicenna's view that the heaven's movement, proceeding from its own soul, directly causes human choice by acting per se upon our souls.
B3C88: No created substance, whether the souls of heavenly bodies or separate intellectual substances, can directly cause or impel our acts of choosing and willing; only God can.
B3C89: Refutes Origen's view that God causes only the will's power to choose, not particular acts of willing, showing instead that God moves the will's very act.
B3C90: It follows from the foregoing that human choice and will, though free, remain entirely subject to and governed by divine providence in all their movements.
B3C91: Explains how human affairs, though seemingly haphazard, can rightly be referred to higher causes under divine providence and thus do not happen by mere chance.
B3C92: Explains in what sense a man may be called fortunate, and how such good fortune arises from the assistance and disposition of higher governing causes.
B3C93: Investigates the question of fate, distinguishing the truth in the notion of ordered secondary causes governing contingent events from the false necessity ascribed to fate by some.
B3C94: Addresses the difficulty that if all contingent events are subject to providence, providence must seem either uncertain or all things necessary, resolving it through God's eternal mode of knowing.
B3C95: The unchangeableness of divine providence does not exclude the usefulness of prayer, since prayer is itself among the causes providence has ordained to bring about its effects.
B3C96: Continues the argument that providence's unchangeableness leaves prayer meaningful, since we pray not to alter God's plan but that He grant, through prayer, what He foresaw.
B3C97: Shows that things are arranged by divine providence for a definite, intelligible reason, so that the order of the universe reflects God's wisdom rather than arbitrary chance.
B3C98: Distinguishes a universal order comprising all things from particular created orders subordinate to it, explaining how God can act outside a particular order without disorder.
B3C99: God can work outside the order He has imposed on things, producing effects without their usual proximate causes, as demonstrated by the possibility of miracles.
B3C100: What God does beside the ordinary course of nature is nevertheless not contrary to nature, since nature's deepest order remains subject to and obedient to God's will.
B3C102: God alone can work miracles in the strict sense, since only the first cause of all being can produce effects entirely outside the order of created causes.
B3C103: Spiritual substances such as angels or demons can perform wonders, but these, however marvelous, are not miracles properly speaking, since they work within nature's created powers.
B3C104: The wondrous works of magicians do not result merely from the influence of heavenly bodies, contrary to the view that celestial power alone explains such feats.
B3C105: Investigates whence the practices of magic derive their efficacy, concluding that intelligent spiritual substances, not natural or celestial forces alone, are involved in their operation.
B3C106: The intellectual substance lending efficacy to magical practices is not good according to virtue, since its cooperation in deceptive and harmful arts betrays a corrupted will.
B3C107: The intellectual substance assisting in magic arts is not evil by its very nature, since no created intellectual nature can be naturally, essentially evil.
B3C108: Presents arguments that would seem to prove sin is impossible among demons, given their subtle intellectual nature, before Aquinas proceeds to refute this position.
B3C109: Demonstrates from scriptural authority and reasoned argument that sin truly is possible in demons, explaining how their will can turn away from due order.
B3C110: Resolves the earlier objections against sin in demons, explaining that the demon's fall came not from intellectual error but from will failing to consider the higher good.
B3C111: Continuing the account of the demon's sin, shows he departed from virtue's mean not through excess of passion, absent in spirits, but through an inequality of justice.
B3C112: Rational creatures are governed by providence for their own sake, since they have dominion over their acts, whereas other creatures are directed merely as means toward them.
B3C113: The rational creature is directed by God in its actions not only according to its species in general but also with regard for it as an individual.
B3C114: Since rational creatures are governed by God as individuals, it was fitting that man should receive laws directly from God to direct his personal actions.
B3C115: The divine law's chief and primary intention is to direct man above all to union with God, since this union is the principal aim of any lawgiver's rule.
B3C116: Continuing the argument, shows man's mind must be united to God as the divine law's chief aim, since only through subjection to Him is man properly bound.
B3C117: From the divine law's aim of uniting man to God, it follows that this same law also directs man to love his neighbour as a necessary consequence.
B3C118: The divine law binds men to hold the true faith, since a right relationship of love and desire toward God presupposes knowing Him truly rather than in error.
B3C119: Continues arguing for the necessity of true faith, since one who errs about God's nature does not truly know, love, or desire Him as his last end.
B3C120: Continues discussing man's natural inclination to worship, arguing that by natural instinct man feels obliged to show reverence to God, the source of his being and every good.
B3C121: The divine law directs man according to reason in his use of corporeal and sensible things, guiding proper enjoyment of bodily goods so they serve rather than hinder his end.
B3C122: Refutes the view that simple fornication between consenting unattached persons is no sin, showing it wrongs the natural order and future offspring intended by marriage.
B3C123: Argues from the good of offspring and mutual fidelity that matrimony, the lasting union of male and female, should endure not merely for a time but throughout life.
B3C124: Continues arguing for marriage's indissolubility, showing it fosters constant mutual love, careful household provision, and prevents quarrels arising from a wife's abandonment by her husband.
B3C125: Continues arguing against polygamy, showing that having several wives removes certainty of offspring and reduces wives to a servile rather than freely loving status.
B3C126: Continues condemning marriage among close kindred, explaining that while natural law fits the majority of cases, lawgivers may dispense in exceptional individual circumstances.
B3C127: No food is in itself sinful to eat, since consuming food that nourishes the body according to reason's due order fulfills food's proper natural purpose.
B3C128: Since other men are the most useful of all things to man, a social animal, the divine law instructs man to treat his neighbours according to right reason.
B3C129: Shows that many acts prescribed by the divine law are right not merely because commanded, but by their very nature, independent of the positive law's enactment.
B3C130: Continues on acts naturally right or wrong, arguing that whatever hinders reason's proper functioning, such as drunkenness, gluttony, and unchecked passion, is evil by nature.
B3C131: Refutes the error of Vigilantius and others who condemned voluntary poverty embraced for the Gospel, presenting and preparing to answer their arguments against it.
B3C132: Surveys the various ways of life followed by those who embrace voluntary poverty, such as communal ownership or reliance on alms, in preparation for evaluating each.
B3C133: Explains how poverty is good, arguing external riches, though a secondary good serving virtue, are not indispensable, so their voluntary renunciation can itself be virtuous.
B3C134: Answers the earlier arguments against poverty, showing that not every individual need personally gather life's necessities, just as not every bee gathers honey.
B3C135: Resolves objections against the specific ways of life of voluntary poverty, explaining the Apostles' communal Jerusalem arrangement and its historical, provisional circumstances.
B3C136: Presents the errors of those who condemn perpetual continence, listing their arguments against this state of life before Aquinas proceeds to refute them.
B3C137: Continues presenting and preparing to refute arguments against perpetual continence, a repetition of the discussion begun regarding those who impugn this state of perfection.
B3C138: Responds to those who mock the binding of oneself by vow, arguing that necessity imposed by a good and freely chosen vow does not diminish virtue's merit.
B3C139: Shows that neither meritorious deeds nor sins are all equal, since counsels like poverty and continence surpass ordinary licit use of goods and marriage in excellence.
B3C140: Continues distinguishing mortal from other sin, explaining that sins opposed to the last end and to love of God and neighbour are properly called mortal.
B3C141: Explains the difference and hierarchical order among punishments, showing that just as rewards correspond to goods, punishments must correspond in kind to the goods they deprive.
B3C142: Since acts of virtue and sin admit of degrees, divine justice likewise demands that punishments and rewards not all be equal but proportioned to the deed's gravity.
B3C143: Distinguishes mortal from venial sin by their relation to man's last end, explaining that mortal sin's punishment concerns forfeiting that end, unlike venial sin's lesser penalty.
B3C144: Because mortal sin turns a man wholly from his last end, and this end cannot be regained after death, the resulting punishment for mortal sin must be eternal.
B3C145: Continues the argument for the eternity of punishment due to mortal sin, showing such unending penalty preserves the right order that manifests God's wisdom and justice.
B3C146: It is lawful for human judges to inflict punishments on the wicked, since imposing deserved sensible penalties on earth rightly supports divine providence's governance of justice.
B3C147: Continues discussing lawful punishment, distinguishing killing done from unjust anger, forbidden by Christ, from killing done through zeal for justice or to protect the innocent.
B3C148: The assistance of divine grace, though described in Scripture as drawing, leading, or pressing man, does not compel him to virtue against his own free will.
B3C149: Man is unable to merit the first divine assistance that turns him toward good, since like matter awaiting a mover, he cannot move himself to acquire that grace.
B3C150: Since God's assistance is given prior to and independent of human merit, it is fittingly called grace, and explains what is meant specifically by sanctifying grace.
B3C151: Sanctifying grace, as an effect of God's own love in man, causes in the soul the reciprocal love of God, since love naturally seeks love returned.
B3C152: Because grace causes charity in the soul, it likewise follows that grace also causes faith in us, enabling the soul's assent to revealed divine truth.
B3C153: In like manner, divine grace must also cause hope in the soul, the confident expectation of future beatitude grounded in trust in God's assisting power.
B3C154: Discusses the gifts of gratuitous grace, treating especially the divinations of demons and the necessity that revealed matters of faith proceed ultimately from God who sees them.
B3C155: Continues on gratuitous graces, distinguishing lasting habitual gifts necessary throughout a Christian's life, such as faith and charity, from transient gifts like prophecy or miracles.
B3C156: He who falls from grace through sin can, by the renewed assistance of grace, recover and be restored again to the state of righteousness.
B3C157: Man cannot rise from mortal sin and be freed from it except by the assistance of grace, since sin cannot be overcome by unaided natural power alone.
B3C158: Explains how man is freed from sin, requiring both repentance and a firm purpose of amendment, along with penitential suffering that reorients the will contrary to sin's pleasure.
B3C159: Continues on satisfaction for sin, showing intense love of God and contrition can lessen or remove due punishment, and that one may even satisfy vicariously for another.
B3C160: A man already in sin cannot, by his own unaided power, avoid all further sin without grace, since a mind turned from rectitude tends readily back toward evil.
B3C161: God delivers some sinners from sin by His mercy while justly leaving others in their sins, a distinction resting on God's simple will rather than on merit.
B3C162: God is in no way the cause of any man's sinning, since sin's defect arises from the deficient created will, not from God who is the first agent.
B3C163: Treats of predestination, reprobation, and divine election, showing that from eternity God has ordained some to grace and glory while justly permitting others to fail of it.
